Gratuitous
gra-tū´ĭ-tŭs
adj. (given freely, without price and without cause in the receiver)
Latin gratuitus, free, from gratia, favour. The Reformers' standing phrase is gratuitous justification — a righteousness given for nothing, and the Authorized Version's word for it is freely.

Biblical Definition

A gratuitous gift is one with no price and no cause in the receiver. Paul: “being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24) — the Greek adverb means as a gift, for nothing, and is the same word the Lord uses in “freely ye have received, freely give” (Mat 10:8). The invitation keeps the term: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isa 55:1); and the last page of Scripture, “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Rev 22:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines gratuitous as free; voluntary; not required by justice; given without an equivalent; asserted or taken without proof.

expand to see more

GRATUITOUS, a. Free; voluntary; not required by justice; granted without claim or merit; as a gratuitous payment.

2. Asserted or taken without proof; as a gratuitous assumption.

Key Scripture

Rom 3:24 — "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:"

Mat 10:8 — "Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give."

Isa 55:1 — "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."

Rev 22:17 — "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

Rom 5:15 — "But not as the offence, so also is the free gift. For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, which is by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many."

Modern Corruption

Grace is offered on terms, and the Greek adverb behind justified freely is the word for what is given as a gift and costs the receiver nothing.

expand to see more

The Greek word in Romans 3:24 is dorean, and its plainest use in the New Testament is John 15:25, where it is translated without a cause: they hated me without a cause. Set the two verses together and the doctrine is exact. Christ was hated gratuitously — for no reason in Him — and the sinner is justified gratuitously, for no reason in him. In both directions the cause lies outside the person it falls on, and that is what the Reformers meant by gratuitous justification: not that it cost nothing, since it cost the blood, but that it cost the receiver nothing and was earned by nothing in him.

The corruption is never a flat denial; it is the quiet addition of a term. Grace is free, and you must be sincere; free, and you must persevere in order to have deserved it; free, and there is a small charge for the sacraments, the indulgence, the pledge, the level of commitment. Isaiah 55:1 was written against every such tariff, and the strangest word in it is buy: come ye, buy, and eat, without money and without price. The sinner comes as a purchaser to a market where the price has been paid, and the only qualification named in the verse is thirst.

The abuse on the other side is to conclude that a gift costing the receiver nothing therefore asks nothing of him. Matthew 10:8 refuses it in five words: freely ye have received, freely give. The gratuitous character of the gift is the pattern for the disciple's whole conduct with it — he was healed for nothing and heals for nothing, was forgiven a debt he could not pay and forgives a hundred pence. A man who has genuinely received gratuitously becomes recognisable, and the sign is not what he has stopped doing but what he has stopped charging for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dorean (G1432), freely, as a gift, without cause; charis (G5485), grace; dorea (G1431), a free gift; Hebrew chinnam (H2600), for nothing, without price.

expand to see more

Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, as a gift; Romans 3:24, Matthew 10:8, Revelation 21:6, 22:17; and without a cause, John 15:25.

Greek dorea (G1431) — a free gift; Romans 5:15, 5:17, Ephesians 3:7, Acts 2:38.

Hebrew chinnam (H2600) — for nought, without price; Isaiah 52:3, 55:1, Genesis 29:15.

Usage

"“Justified freely by his grace” — the same word rendered without a cause when they hated Him."

"“Buy wine and milk without money and without price” — a purchase where the only qualification is thirst."

"“Freely ye have received, freely give” — the gift becomes the pattern."
